subject: history
title: Elizabethans 1580-1603
final_note: You worked through the key terms in Elizabethans 1580-1603.

concepts.def: Elizabeth ruled through her court, a Privy Council guided by ministers such as William Cecil (Lord Burghley), and occasional Parliaments.
Catholics who refused to attend Anglican services faced heavy fines after 1581, while missionary priests such as Edmund Campion were executed as traitors.
The Catholic claimant held captive in England; evidence of her involvement in the Babington Plot led to her execution at Fotheringhay in 1587.
Philip II's invasion fleet was scattered by English fireships at Calais and shattered by storms as it fled around Scotland and Ireland.
Rising population and the terrible harvests of the 1590s increased vagrancy, and the 1601 Poor Law made each parish responsible for its own poor.
A flourishing of drama, music and exploration, with playhouses such as the Globe (1599) and voyagers like Drake, although life stayed harsh for most people.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Elizabethans 1580-1603 — a core area of GCSE History.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Elizabethans 1580-1603 brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Elizabethans 1580-1603.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Why was Mary, Queen of Scots executed in 1587?
options: Evidence implicated her in the Babington Plot to assassinate Elizabeth
She had claimed the throne of France
She refused to convert to Catholicism
She led the Spanish Armada against England

mcqs.q: What helped defeat the Spanish Armada in 1588?
options: Fireships scattered the fleet at Calais and storms wrecked many ships on the voyage home
The Spanish fleet ran out of food before leaving Spain
A French fleet destroyed the Armada in the Channel
English troops captured the Armada's ports in Spain

mcqs.q: What did the 1601 Poor Law require?
options: Parishes to collect a poor rate to support their own deserving poor
All poor people to enter royal workhouses
Monasteries to feed the poor of every town
The Crown to pay pensions to all unemployed people

mcqs.q: Which playhouse, associated with Shakespeare's company, opened in London in 1599?
options: The Globe
The Rose
The Swan
The Curtain

mcqs.q: Did the English navy sink most of the Spanish Armada in battle?
options: The Poor Laws abolished poverty in England by 1603.
No - relatively few Spanish ships were sunk in the fighting; most losses came from storms that wrecked ships sailing home around Scotland and Ireland.
Drake destroyed the Armada in one decisive sea battle.
The Armada was defeated because Spain had no warships left after 1580.

mcqs.q: Were all Elizabethan Catholics plotting against the queen?
options: Every Catholic in Elizabethan England supported plots to kill Elizabeth.
No - most English Catholics stayed loyal; harsh laws targeted missionary priests and recusants, but actual plots involved only a small minority.
The Poor Laws abolished poverty in England by 1603.
Catholicism was unknown in England by the 1580s.

mcqs.q: Did the Elizabethan Poor Laws punish everyone who was poor?
options: No - they distinguished the 'deserving' poor, helped by parish relief, from able-bodied 'idle' vagrants, who could be punished or set to work.
The Armada was defeated because Spain had no warships left after 1580.
Elizabethans whipped or imprisoned all poor people equally.
The Poor Laws abolished poverty in England by 1603.
